threads.successCriteria: Nakasendo / Kiso Valley is locked as the hiking anchor with a concrete route (Magome–Tsumago–Nagiso, optional Narai/Yabuhara), day-by-day distances and post-town lodging, and rail + luggage-forwarding logistics that connect Tokyo and Kyoto without a major detour.
threads.rationale: Anchoring on the Nakasendo keeps the hiking on the existing Tokyo–Kyoto corridor, so it adds scenery and a cultural high point without forcing a separate side-trip — unlike alternatives such as the Kumano Kodo (far south, needs its own loop) or Kamikochi/Japan Alps (a northern detour off the main line). Structuring the plan as 'lock the segment → define days/distances → fit transport → book lodging' front-loads the decision that everything else depends on, so later booking and logistics steps don't have to be redone.

tasks.description: Lock Nakasendo / Kiso Valley as the hiking anchor and define the core route: Magome → Tsumago → Nagiso, with Narai/Yabuhara as an optional extension. Note why this beats alternatives (on Tokyo–Kyoto corridor, minimal detour).
Set the number of hiking days and daily distances/stages, including where the optional extension day fits and the daily walking hours and elevation profile for each stage.
Choose post-town lodging (ryokan/minshuku/guesthouse) in Magome, Tsumago, and/or Nagiso, matched to the day stages, and identify booking windows for peak seasons.

Fit the segment into the Tokyo–Kyoto route: rail access (Chuo/Shinano lines, Limited Express Shinano via Nagoya or Nagano), station-to-trailhead transfers, and luggage forwarding (takuhaibin) so bags skip the trail.
Prepare on-trail logistics and contingencies: Nakasendo waymarker route maps, seasonal weather check, bear bells, cash for post towns, and a fallback plan if a stage is rained out.
